```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", dev = "png",
                      fig.retina = 2, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.4,
                      fig.align = "center")
library(mlvtoolbox)
okabe <- c(blue = "#0072B2", orange = "#E69F00", vermillion = "#D55E00")
```

`mlvtoolbox` is a corrected port of the Mid-Level Vision (MLV) toolbox, the
MATLAB code of the Bernhardt-Walther lab described by Walther et al. (2023).
Its defaults fix defects found in that code while qualifying the port against
outputs the lab computed in MATLAB. Some of those fixes change the numbers,
which matters when you want to compare new data with published MLV values or
rerun a published analysis. For that case the package keeps a
*published-compatible mode*: explicit `mlv2023` options that reproduce the
MATLAB results, defects included.

This vignette gives the exact recipe for each mode, lists what each correction
changes and why, shows on small synthetic drawings where the two modes differ
and where they agree, shows how feature specifications keep the two apart, and
summarizes the qualification evidence. It ends with a short guide to choosing
a mode and describing it in a methods section.

## The two modes

The *corrected defaults* need no arguments. The *published-compatible mode*
sets five options, on two functions:

```{r recipe, eval = FALSE}
# Junctions
detect_junctions(drawing, rule = "mlv2023")      # implies gap_metric = "chebyshev"

# Medial axis
compute_mat(drawing, aof = "mlv2023", morphology = "hmt8", branch_rule = "mlv2023",
            threshold_angle = asin(0.3 * pi / 2) * 180 / pi)  # 28.11°, flux threshold 0.3 (MLV-M004)
```

`analyse_mat()` passes the medial-axis options through to `compute_mat()`,
and `compute_mat_properties()` and `map_mat_properties()` follow the
`branch_rule` recorded in the `mlv_mat`. The threshold angle is explained
below. Contour orientation, length and curvature need no option: the
published contour estimator (`estimator = "mlv2023"` in `feature_spec()`) is
the default in both modes.

A feature specification declares the same choices once, so that every
function that measures a drawing uses them:

```{r specs}
angle_03 <- asin(0.3 * pi / 2) * 180 / pi   # 28.11°, flux threshold 0.3
props <- c("orientation", "length", "curvature", "junction_type",
           "parallelism", "separation", "mirror")
corrected <- feature_spec(props, bins = 4)
published <- feature_spec(props, bins = 4,
  junction = list(rule = "mlv2023"),
  mat = list(aof = "mlv2023", morphology = "hmt8", branch_rule = "mlv2023",
             threshold_angle = angle_03))
knitr::kable(data.frame(corrected = corrected$definitions,
                        published = published$definitions))
```

Every specification records a versioned *definition* for each method. The
table shows that the two modes differ in five of them (AOF, morphology, branch
rule, junction rule and branch tracing) and share the contour, branch-score and
histogram definitions.

### Why the recipe sets the threshold angle

The stored MLV datasets were computed by `computeAllMATfromVecLD.m`, which
calls `computeMAT.m` without a threshold, so MATLAB used its fallback flux
threshold of 0.3. The package derives the threshold from an object angle,
(2/π) sin(`threshold_angle`), and its default angle of 28° gives
`r format(2 / pi * sin(28 * pi / 180), digits = 6)`, not 0.3 (MLV-M004). The
qualification runs that reproduced the stored values therefore passed the
angle whose threshold is exactly 0.3:

```{r threshold}
angle_03
published$settings$mat$threshold_angle == angle_03
m <- compute_mat(mlv_drawing(list(matrix(c(5, 10, 45, 10), 1),
                                  matrix(c(5, 22, 45, 22), 1)), 50, 32),
                 spec = published)
m$parameters$threshold
```

With the default angle, pixels whose flux lies between the two thresholds
(17.93 and 18 of a possible 60 at 60 samples) enter the skeleton although
MATLAB excluded them. How often that happens on natural drawings has not
been measured; use the full recipe when you need the stored values.

## What each correction changes

Each default corrects a behaviour of the pinned MATLAB source (commit
`f12418a`) that is demonstrated by a synthetic reproducer with an
independently derived answer. The identifiers refer to the
[upstream bug register](https://github.com/bbuchsbaum/mlvtoolboxR/blob/main/UPSTREAM_BUGS.md),
which gives the reproducer and the number of affected items in the stored
datasets for each.

| Stage | MLV behaviour, reproduced by `mlv2023` | Corrected default | ID |
|---|---|---|---|
| Junction merging and angles | Merging depends on the order of the intersections; interior arms use a different y convention from endpoint arms; intersections at negative coordinates are discarded | Transitive merging; one angle convention; any coordinates | M006–M008 |
| Junction gap | A 1 px gap allowance measured along the larger coordinate change, so up to 1.41 px on a diagonal | Euclidean gap (`gap_metric = "euclidean"`), the same in every direction | M018 |
| Junction position | Intersections within 1e-4 of a segment end snap to the endpoint | Exact intersection | M019 |
| Junction arms | Arms of interior segments measured from the merged junction centroid | Direction of the segment through which the contour leaves | M021 |
| Junction arms | A segment attaches by its start if that lies within 2 px, so reversing a contour can change the junction | Arms are the exits of each contour from the junction neighbourhood, independent of direction | M022 |
| Junction arms | Splitting one stroke into two contours with a short middle piece creates a junction | Contours ending inside the neighbourhood contribute no arm | M023 |
| Junction arms | Every segment of a contour inside the neighbourhood counts as an arm; a slight overshoot reads as X | One arm per exit | M024, M025 |
| Junction arms | Closed contours end at their first vertex | Closed contours wrap around | M026 |
| Flux | Sampling circle centred on the pixel corner, labels read from the containing cell: ridges displaced by half a pixel | Circle centred on the pixel, mean over equidistant boundary pixels (`aof = "centered"`) | M027 |
| Thinning | MATLAB `bwmorph("skel", Inf)`, reproduced by `morphology = "hmt8"`; can leave removable pixels and 2 x 2 blocks | `morphology = "minimal"`: no removable pixel remains | not an MLV defect |
| Branch scores | Forward differences: scores depend on the direction in which a branch was traced | Mean over both directions (`branch_rule = "invariant"`) | M028 |
| Mapping | Scores read from a last-writer-wins image; exact nearest-point ties broken by enumeration order | Each branch keeps its own scores; ties take the maximum | M029 |
| Tracing | Junction points duplicated when edges are merged | No point repeated within a branch | M030 |
| Mirror score | The line fit forces the last one or two points into the final span even when that exceeds the 1 px error tolerance | The fit stops before the failing point | M016 |
| Mapping | Every mapped score of exactly zero treated as missing | Valid zeros kept; missing is NA | M011 |

The thinning row is a choice rather than a defect: `"hmt8"` is the thinning
that reproduces MATLAB's skeleton, and the default removes the pixels it
leaves that are not needed to keep the skeleton connected.

Two behaviours are corrected in both modes, because reproducing them would
produce invalid values rather than different ones: separation is NA below a
radius of 1 pixel instead of exceeding 1 or becoming infinite (M031), and
zero-length segments are rejected or dropped instead of producing undefined
angles and curvatures (M015, M020).

## Where the modes agree and where they differ

The drawing below has a long bar, a stem that meets it from below and a
separate short line.

```{r drawing}
seg <- function(...) matrix(c(...), nrow = 1)
drawing <- mlv_drawing(list(
  seg(10, 20, 70, 20),
  rbind(c(40, 44, 40, 21.5), c(40, 21.5, 40, 20)),
  seg(10, 32, 30, 32)), width = 80, height = 50)
```

### Contour geometry is identical

Orientation, length and curvature do not depend on the mode:

```{r geometry}
table_corrected <- feature_table(analyse_mat(drawing, spec = corrected)$drawing)
table_published <- feature_table(analyse_mat(drawing, spec = published)$drawing)
geometry <- grep("^(orientation|length|curvature)_", names(table_corrected), value = TRUE)
identical(table_corrected[geometry], table_published[geometry])
```

### Junctions

Junctions differ wherever one of MLV's arm rules applies, for example when a
short segment at the end of a stem makes a T read as an X (MLV-M024).
`vignette("junctions", package = "mlvtoolbox")` shows each case on a small
drawing.

### Medial-axis scores differ by design

The medial-axis corrections change values at many pixels, because they
move the ridge (M027), average the two traversal directions (M028) and change
how scores reach the contour (M029, M030). Per-contour means remain
correlated across modes. The comparison below uses eight random synthetic
drawings of eight polylines each.

```{r random}
set.seed(2023)
random_drawing <- function(n = 8, size = 100) {
  contours <- lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
    k <- sample(2:4, 1)
    p <- matrix(runif(2 * k, 8, size - 8), ncol = 2)
    cbind(p[-k, , drop = FALSE], p[-1, , drop = FALSE])
  })
  mlv_drawing(contours, size, size)
}
P <- c("parallelism", "separation", "mirror")
contour_means <- function(d, ...) {
  x <- analyse_mat(d, properties = P, ...)$drawing
  sapply(P, function(p) vapply(x$mat_properties[[p]], mean, double(1), na.rm = TRUE))
}
drawings <- replicate(8, random_drawing(), simplify = FALSE)
a <- do.call(rbind, lapply(drawings, contour_means))
b <- do.call(rbind, lapply(drawings, contour_means, aof = "mlv2023",
                           morphology = "hmt8", branch_rule = "mlv2023",
                           threshold_angle = angle_03))
ok <- stats::complete.cases(a, b)
c(contours = nrow(a), compared = sum(ok))
r <- sapply(P, function(p) cor(a[ok, p], b[ok, p]))
round(r, 3)
```

```{r fig-random, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 2.7, fig.cap = sprintf("Per-contour mean scores in the published-compatible mode (x) and the corrected defaults (y) for %d contours of eight random synthetic drawings, with the identity line in grey. The modes are correlated (r = %.2f, %.2f and %.2f here) but rarely give the same value.", sum(ok), r[1], r[2], r[3])}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(3.2, 3.4, 2, 0.8), mgp = c(2, 0.5, 0),
          las = 1, cex.axis = 0.8, cex.lab = 0.85, cex.main = 1, font.main = 1)
for (p in P) {
  plot(b[ok, p], a[ok, p], xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), asp = 1,
       pch = 16, cex = 0.7, col = adjustcolor(okabe[["blue"]], 0.7),
       xlab = "published-compatible", ylab = "corrected default", main = p, bty = "l")
  abline(0, 1, col = "grey60")
}
par(op)
```

For these random drawings the per-contour correlations between modes are
`r round(r[["parallelism"]], 2)` (parallelism), `r round(r[["separation"]], 2)`
(separation) and `r round(r[["mirror"]], 2)` (mirror). Random line segments
make many short, irregular branches, so these values say nothing about natural
drawings; the qualification figures for natural drawings are in the evidence
section below.

### Valid zeros

The corrected mode keeps scores that are exactly zero; the published mode,
like `MATpropertiesToContours.m`, turns every zero into a missing value
(MLV-M011). Two lines three pixels apart have a separation of exactly 0 along
their whole length (`vignette("medial-axis", package = "mlvtoolbox")` explains
why), so the same pixels are zeros in one mode and missing in the other:

```{r zeros}
close_pair <- mlv_drawing(list(seg(10, 20, 50, 20), seg(10, 23, 50, 23)), 60, 40)
separation <- function(...) {
  x <- analyse_mat(close_pair, ...)$drawing
  v <- unlist(x$mat_properties$separation)
  c(zero = sum(v == 0, na.rm = TRUE), missing = sum(is.na(v)))
}
rbind(corrected = separation(),
      published = separation(aof = "mlv2023", morphology = "hmt8",
                             branch_rule = "mlv2023", threshold_angle = angle_03))
```

## Specifications keep the modes apart

A feature specification travels with the measurements it produced. Functions
that accept one check that the inputs they receive were computed under the
same definitions and stop otherwise, so values from the two modes cannot be
combined by accident. A medial axis computed in published mode cannot be
scored under the corrected specification:

```{r reject-mat, error = TRUE}
published_mat <- compute_mat(drawing, spec = published)
compute_mat_properties(published_mat, spec = corrected)
```

Scores computed under one specification cannot be mapped under the other:

```{r reject-scores, error = TRUE}
scored <- compute_mat_properties(compute_mat(drawing, spec = published), spec = published)
map_mat_properties(drawing, scored, spec = corrected)
```

A specification is also checked against the definitions that the installed
version produces for its settings. Specifications saved by mlvtoolbox 0.2.x
recorded the thinning then in use, the Octave Pratt lookup tables, and had no
AOF or branch-rule definitions; such a specification is rejected rather than
silently reinterpreted. The example below changes one recorded definition to
the 0.2.x value:

```{r reject-old, error = TRUE}
old <- corrected
old$definitions[["morphology"]] <- "octave_image_pratt_2.20.0"
validate_feature_spec(old)
```

Rebuild such a specification with `feature_spec()` and recompute the cached
medial axes from the drawings.

## Qualification evidence

The numbers in this section are results of the qualification run recorded in
[`docs/PARITY.md`](https://github.com/bbuchsbaum/mlvtoolboxR/blob/main/docs/PARITY.md)
and the reports it links. They are not recomputed here, because the reference
data are the lab's natural drawings, which are not distributed with the
package.

The reference set holds outputs computed in MATLAB for 3,017 line drawings
(IAPS, OASIS, architectural scenes, Toronto scenes and Snodgrass-Vanderwart
drawings), 2,757 of them with per-pixel parallelism, separation and mirror
scores, plus the complete distance map, flux and skeleton of one drawing
(Forest_DBW). Rerunning the pinned MATLAB source (f12418a) under GNU Octave
reproduced every stored geometry value and all junctions checked, so the
stored outputs correspond to that source revision.

| Stage | Published-compatible mode vs stored MATLAB | Corrected defaults vs stored MATLAB |
|---|---|---|
| Segment orientation, length, curvature | All 2,284,239 segments within 1e-9 | Same |
| Junctions | 395,125 of 395,134 identical in position, type, members and angles; the other 9 depend on zero-length segments | 356,113 (90.1%) identical; every difference attributed to a named defect or definition |
| Distance map, flux, skeleton (Forest_DBW) | Distances identical, flux within 2.1e-14, skeleton identical (24,904 px) | Different by design (M027, thinning) |
| Per-pixel scores (2,757 drawings) | 99.1%, 99.4% and 99.3% of pixels within 1e-4 (parallelism, separation, mirror); per-contour r = 0.9993, 0.9999, 0.9986 | Per-contour r = 0.889, 0.972, 0.836 |

The remaining per-pixel differences in published mode come from MLV's
single-precision arithmetic, which occasionally flips an exact tie between
nearest tangent points. The qualification has stated limits: MATLAB itself
was not run, so the stored outputs serve as the reference; MATLAB's
undocumented skeletonization was identified empirically and matched exactly
on the Forest_DBW drawing; rasterization tie rules were observed only for
integer endpoints; and extracting drawings from photographs is not qualified.

## Choosing a mode

Use the **corrected defaults** for new studies. Their junctions and
medial-axis scores do not depend on contour direction, contour numbering, the
start vertex of a closed contour or the direction in which a branch was
traced, and rotating or reflecting the ink raster by a multiple of 90° rotates
or reflects the flux field in the same way. The corrected defaults keep the
published contour curvature estimator; for new studies also consider
`feature_spec(estimator = "arclength", curvature_scale = ...)`, which defines
curvature at a stated physical scale (see
`vignette("getting-started", package = "mlvtoolbox")`).

Use the **published-compatible mode** when values must be comparable with
numbers computed by the MATLAB toolbox: extending or replicating a published
dataset, comparing against published norms, or rerunning an analysis whose
features were computed in MATLAB. Do not mix modes within one analysis; save
the feature specification with the data, and the checks above enforce this.

If a result depends on the mode, report both. Contour geometry is identical
in the two modes, most junctions are identical, and per-contour medial-axis
means are highly correlated but not equal, so an effect that appears in only
one mode deserves a closer look at the drawings that drive it.

### Describing the mode in a methods section

Report the package version, the mode and the settings that differ from the
defaults, and cite both the package and the original methods. `citation()`
gives the references:

```{r citation, comment = ""}
print(citation("mlvtoolbox"), style = "text")
```

Example sentence for the corrected defaults:

> Contour orientation, length, curvature, junctions and medial-axis
> parallelism, separation and mirror symmetry were computed with mlvtoolbox
> `r packageVersion("mlvtoolbox")` (Buchsbaum, 2026), an R implementation of
> the Mid-Level Vision Toolbox (Walther et al., 2023), using its default
> definitions, which correct documented defects of the MATLAB implementation;
> medial-axis scores follow Rezanejad et al. (2019).

Example sentence for the published-compatible mode:

> Features were computed with mlvtoolbox `r packageVersion("mlvtoolbox")`
> (Buchsbaum, 2026) in its published-compatible mode (junction rule `mlv2023`;
> medial axis with `aof = "mlv2023"`, `morphology = "hmt8"`,
> `branch_rule = "mlv2023"` and an object-angle threshold of 28.11°, that is,
> a flux threshold of 0.3), which reproduces the values of the MATLAB
> Mid-Level Vision Toolbox (Walther et al., 2023; source revision f12418a).

If you used a nondefault threshold, window or mapping radius, state it, and
deposit the feature specification (for example as the sidecar written by
`write_feature_csv()`) with the data.
